rounds.title: Ask before dividing
rounds.situation: A hospital or university site has 40 parking spaces and around 70 staff who drive to work. Staff on early and late shifts want a fixed allocation of reserved parking spaces; some have no safe alternative to driving at those hours. Management has refused a fixed, named allocation because the site layout may change next year and it wants flexibility. Both negotiating sides are preparing to argue about how many parking spaces to reserve.

cards.title: Ask what matters
cards.text: Paraphrase the demand, then ask what problem the requested number would solve.
cards.why: Diagnosis helps distinguish a stated position from the need beneath it.

cards.title: Explore different priorities
cards.text: Ask which times, uses or conditions matter most to each side.
cards.why: Different priorities may allow value without conceding the opening demand.

cards.title: Split the number immediately
cards.text: Offer half before asking about the problem.
cards.why: A quick compromise can leave the underlying needs untouched.

rounds.task: You have five minutes to open the negotiation. Choose two moves that help clarify what matters to each side before making an offer.

rounds.title: Agree the measure
rounds.situation: At a pay-negotiation meeting, management uses a wage-bill percentage to argue that a pay increase is unaffordable. Staff representatives cite a lower percentage and say there is room for an increase. The figures come from different documents. Neither team has explained which pay costs, institutions, revenue base or reporting period its calculation covers. The discussion is stuck on which number is right.

cards.title: Define the denominator
cards.text: Agree the institutions, revenue basis, time period and wage components.
cards.why: Numbers can differ because their definitions differ.

cards.title: Check the source
cards.text: Ask for the publication, date and assumptions behind each figure.
cards.why: A verifiable source makes an affordability argument testable.

cards.title: Average the percentages
cards.text: Use the midpoint without investigating the definitions.
cards.why: Averaging incompatible measures does not establish a valid measure.

rounds.task: Choose two moves to establish whether the figures can be compared before using them to support a pay proposal.

rounds.title: Find the authority
rounds.situation: Management and staff representatives are negotiating a six-month pilot for a new staff rota. A rota is the schedule showing who works which shifts. The staff delegation's instructions require monthly reviews of the pilot; the management delegation may agree only to quarterly reviews. Neither team has authority to change its instructions. Other details are close to agreement, and there is pressure to promise a different review interval so the meeting can finish.

cards.title: Clarify the limits
cards.text: State the conflict in mandates and identify who can authorize a change.
cards.why: A visible gap in authority is a preparation issue, not something to conceal.

cards.title: Seek a revised mandate
cards.text: Propose a caucus or a dated referral to the principals with a specific option.
cards.why: A lawful route to revised authority can reopen the space for agreement.

cards.title: Sign a convenient compromise
cards.text: Promise a different interval without consulting either principal.
cards.why: A promise outside the mandate may fail at implementation.

rounds.task: Choose two moves to handle the gap in authority and establish a route to an authorised decision.

rounds.title: Protect a safe voice
rounds.situation: At a meeting in a hospital or university teaching laboratory, staff representatives raise a concern about possible exposure to infectious biological samples. They want a clear way to report incidents and follow-up on the hazard. A manager offers an allowance for the affected work but asks staff to remove the reporting concern from the agenda. The proposal does not explain how exposure would be controlled or who would act on reports.

cards.title: Protect reporting
cards.text: Agree a safe reporting route and action on the hazard through the responsible process.
cards.why: Reporting and hazard prevention must be addressed, not replaced by payment.

cards.title: Involve the right people
cards.text: Include appropriate worker representation and those responsible for prevention and implementation.
cards.why: Voice and technical responsibility support a workable preventive response.

cards.title: Trade silence for payment
cards.text: Accept the allowance if staff stop raising the safety concern.
cards.why: An allowance does not remove the hazard or the need for protection.

rounds.task: Choose two moves to respond to the proposed exchange and address the staff's concern through the appropriate people and process.

rounds.title: Lower the temperature
rounds.situation: A union-management meeting about a proposed change to working hours has become tense. A delegate points to differences between figures circulated before the meeting and those being used now, and calls the other team dishonest. That team says the earlier figures were preliminary. Delegates start interrupting and defending their reputations, and the discussion moves away from the proposal. The disputed information still needs attention.

cards.title: Acknowledge and check
cards.text: Recognize the concern, paraphrase the disputed point and ask for the evidence.
cards.why: Acknowledgement can reduce defensiveness without conceding the substance.

cards.title: Take a purposeful pause
cards.text: Call a short break and agree what each side will clarify before returning.
cards.why: A structured pause can restore attention and internal coordination.

cards.title: Match the volume
cards.text: Interrupt more loudly so your side is not seen as weak.
cards.why: Matching escalation makes clear listening and decisions harder.

rounds.task: Choose two moves to respond to the accusation and help the teams return to a workable discussion.

rounds.title: Make it implementable
rounds.situation: After a long meeting, management and staff representatives appear to agree on additional staff training and a related allowance. Some participants understand that it will start next month; others believe it depends on budget approval. The amount, eligibility, funding source and date for reviewing the arrangement have not been recorded clearly. There are ten minutes left, and both sides are keen to announce a successful agreement.

cards.title: Read back the specifics
cards.text: Confirm what, who, amount, date, unresolved issues and the written record.
cards.why: Specific terms expose misunderstandings while there is time to correct them.

cards.title: Check implementation authority
cards.text: Confirm lawful funding, necessary approvals, registration where required and a review point.
cards.why: The people at the table may not control every implementation step.

cards.title: Close with a handshake
cards.text: Leave the details for later because the atmosphere is good.
cards.why: Goodwill alone cannot define or fund an implementable agreement.

rounds.task: Choose two moves to establish exactly what has been agreed and what must happen before it can be implemented.
